n: Near the end of his life, David gathers every level of leadership in Israel — tribal heads, army commanders, and the managers of royal property — to Jerusalem for a solemn public handoff of the temple project to Solomon.

f.g: In rotating shifts; 1 Chronicles 27 lists twelve divisions that each served the king one month a year.

n: An old king rising to his feet shows how much this moment matters to him. David calls the people his “brethren” and explains that he had longed to build a resting place for the ark, and had already gathered materials.

f.g: The ark was pictured as the footstool of the invisible divine King enthroned above the cherubim.

n: God had told David no. The temple was to be a house of peace, and David’s life had been spent in war. His disappointment becomes a lesson that God may assign a sacred work to someone else.

f.w: thou hast been a man of war

n: David traces God’s choosing step by step: the tribe of Judah, the family of Jesse, and finally David himself, the youngest son. His kingship was a gift, not an achievement.

f.w: he hath chosen Judah to be the ruler

f.g: He was pleased with me; he took delight in choosing me.

n: Among David’s many sons, God chose Solomon. Notice the phrase “the kingdom of the LORD” — the Chronicler stresses that the true King of Israel is God, and David’s heirs only sit on His throne.

f.w: the throne of the kingdom of the LORD

n: David quotes God’s promise that Solomon would build the temple and be treated as God’s own son. This father–son covenant language later points forward to the Messiah, the greater Son of David.
The promise of a lasting kingdom comes with a condition: Solomon must keep obeying, as he is doing now. God’s blessings in covenant are tied to faithfulness.

f.g: If he remains firm and steady.

n: Turning to the whole assembly, David charges them before both the people and God himself to keep every commandment, so they can keep the promised land and pass it to their children.

f.w: in the audience of our God
f.g: In God’s hearing — He is a witness to this charge.

n: One of the great verses of the Old Testament. David tells Solomon to truly know God and serve Him wholeheartedly and willingly, because God sees every thought. Seek Him and He will be found — forsake Him and lose Him.

f.g: Hebrew lev shalem — a whole, undivided heart; complete loyalty, not flawlessness.

f.w: if thou seek him, he will be found of thee

n: A short, punchy charge: God has chosen you for this — be strong and get it done. Divine calling is paired with personal effort.
David hands Solomon the detailed plan for the temple — its entry porch, buildings, storerooms, upper rooms, and the innermost room where the mercy seat would rest.

f.g: Hebrew tavnit — a model or blueprint, the same word used for the tabernacle plan shown to Moses.

f.w: the place of the mercy seat
f.g: The holy of holies, where the ark’s gold lid symbolized God’s throne of atonement.

n: Importantly, David received this plan “by the spirit.” Like the tabernacle before it, the temple was designed by revelation, not human imagination.

f.g: Or ‘that he had in his spirit/mind’; the Chronicler presents it as revealed.
Spoils and gifts set apart for God’s house.

n: The plan included not only buildings but organization: the rotating divisions of priests and Levites and all the tools for temple worship. Order in God’s house matters as much as architecture.
David even set aside exact weights of gold and silver for each tool. Nothing was left to chance — sacred things were prepared with care and precision.

f.g: Utensils or vessels used in the service.

n: Gold and silver were measured for each lampstand and its lamps. These lights recalled the tabernacle’s menorah, a symbol of God’s presence and light among His people.

f.g: Lampstands holding oil lamps, not wax candles.

n: Gold was given for the tables of shewbread, where loaves were set out before the Lord continually.

f.g: ‘Bread of the Presence’ — twelve loaves kept before God, renewed each Sabbath.

n: Even the smaller utensils — forks for handling meat, bowls, cups, and basins — had their own measured gold or silver. Every part of worship was treated as holy.

f.g: Large forks used to handle sacrificial meat.

n: Refined gold was set aside for the incense altar and for the golden cherubim whose wings overshadowed the ark — pictured here as God’s chariot-throne.

f.g: The cherubim were seen as the throne-chariot of God, as in Ezekiel’s vision.

n: David testifies that the Lord made the plan clear to him in writing, by His hand resting on David. The temple design came by revelation, much as Moses received the tabernacle pattern.

f.g: An idiom for the power of God’s Spirit coming upon a prophet.

n: David repeats the encouragement Moses once gave Joshua: be strong, don’t be afraid, God won’t abandon you until the work is done. It is a promise to anyone given a hard assignment from God.

f.w: he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee

n: Solomon would not work alone: priests, Levites, skilled and willing craftsmen, leaders, and people would all support him. God’s work is a shared effort of willing hearts.
